title: What if gravity flipped for one second?
caption:
One second of flipped gravity would throw you 10 metres up. 🌍⬆️

For that second you'd fall UP the way you normally fall down: 4.9 m, and already moving at about 35 km/h.

When gravity switches back you don't stop. You coast up another 4.9 m, to almost 10 m: about three storeys.

Then the fall: 1.4 seconds, landing at about 50 km/h. Every loose object around you takes the same ride.

The safer spot is indoors: the ceiling stops you after less than a metre.

Inside or outside when it happens? One word 👇

Send this to the friend who'd definitely be outside.

Follow @the.impossible.lab for more impossible science.

⚠️ Don't try this. A fall from 10 m (about three storeys) can be fatal: never jump from heights to "feel" it.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_gravity (standard gravity g0 = 9.80665 m/s², defined value; 9.81 used)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_velocity (skydiver belly-to-earth terminal velocity about 55 m/s: drag at 14 m/s is ~(14/55)² ≈ 6 % of weight, so 'air drag ignored' changes the landing speed by only a few %)

Computed (constant-acceleration kinematics, s = ½gt², v = gt, v² = 2gh): flipped second: s = ½·9.81·1² = 4.905 m, v = 9.81 m/s (35.3 km/h); coast after gravity returns: h = v²/2g = 4.905 m -> peak 9.81 m at t = 2 s; fall from 9.81 m: t = √(2h/g) = 1.41 s, v = √(2gh) = 13.87 m/s = 49.9 km/h
Computed (indoors): ceiling 2.6 m, head top ≈1.8 m -> gap ≈0.8 m, reached after √(2·0.8/9.81) ≈ 0.4 s at ≈4 m/s; dropping back ≈0.8 m after the second ends -> ≈4 m/s, vs ≈13.9 m/s outdoors
